big_case.notes: First district court preliminary injunction blocking IIRIRA section 102(c) border-barrier waivers in two decades, halting construction across the 517-mile Big Bend Sector (including Big Bend National Park) under the $46.5B OBBBA appropriation, and eliciting a published per curiam Supreme Court opinion holding under Dalton v. Specter, Biden v. Nebraska, and FCC v. Consumers' Research that there is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim within section 102(c)(2)(A)'s jurisdiction-stripping exception.

No CourtListener or web calls were made, and no post-cutoff or outcome-revealing material existed or was accessed.

central_claims.basis: On November 9, 2026 (11 days after the October 29 response, following the Government's October 30 reply), Justice Alito referred Application 26A560 to the full Court and the Court granted an unqualified stay pending certiorari without granting summary reversal.
central_claims.claim: The Court will grant the stay of the Western District of Texas preliminary injunction after referral to the full Court, within roughly one to two weeks of the October 29 response following the government's reply, while declining summary reversal.

central_claims.basis: The November 9, 2026 per curiam opinion (`writings/OT2026-2/01-per-curiam.txt`) held that the Government is exceedingly likely to prevail because IIRIRA section 102(c)(2)(A) limits district court jurisdiction to constitutional claims, respondents' major-questions claim alleges only that the Secretary exceeded statutory authority under Dalton v. Specter, 511 U.S. 462, 472-474 (1994), and 'there is no such thing as a 'constitutional' major-questions claim,' without deciding whether Big Bend is an area of high illegal entry.
central_claims.claim: If the Court addresses the merits, the likely ground is IIRIRA section 102(c)(2)(A)'s jurisdictional bar under Dalton v. Specter—that a major-questions argument is a claim of statutory authority rather than a constitutional claim—without deciding whether Big Bend is an 'area of high illegal entry.'

central_claims.basis: The per curiam opinion held that Congress's enactment of IIRIRA section 102(c) reflects a clear preference for expeditious border construction over the aesthetic, recreational, and environmental harms respondents assert, citing United States v. Oakland Cannabis Buyers' Coop. and Winter v. NRDC.
central_claims.claim: The equities favor a stay because respondents' aesthetic and recreational harms do not outweigh the government's border-construction interests.

central_claims.basis: No further response request occurred (`response_requested: true`) and no additional amicus briefs were filed beyond FAIR's October 29 brief (`amicus_briefs: 1`).
central_claims.claim: No further response request will occur, and additional amicus filings beyond FAIR's brief are capped by the short window before disposition.

central_claims.basis: Rather than issuing a short unsigned order, the Court issued a 5-page published per curiam opinion (`writings/OT2026-2/01-per-curiam.txt`), and Justice Jackson noted that she would deny the stay without authoring a separate dissent (`writings.json`).
central_claims.claim: The grant will most likely come in a short unsigned order, with a noted dissent from at least one of Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson (though a dissent from Jackson on the jurisdictional point is less certain given CBD v. McAleenan).
